utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, distinguished members of the Tribunal. It is it my privilege to appear before you on behalf of General Ante Gotovina. This motion seeks the entry of a judgement of acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in relation to all counts in the amended joint indictment. It is our submission that the Prosecutor has provided no evidence capable of supporting a conviction against General Gotovina on any of the counts in the indictment. With your permission, Mr. President, I shall first set forth the applicable standard under Rule 98 bis. I shall then set forth a summary of the Prosecution theory, the legal elements of the crimes and criminal liability as charged in the indictment, and a summary of our factual argument as to why the evidence does not prove those elements beyond a reasonable doubt. Following my pleadings, my colleagues, Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Misetic will elaborate our submissions on the evidence in greater detail. It is settled law that in Rule 98 bis proceedings the applicable test is whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonable Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question. The Rule 98 bis jurisprudence identifies four key elements in the evaluation of the evidence. First, where there is into evidence to sustain a charge, the motion is to be allowed; second, where there is some evidence, but it is such that taken at his highest a Trial Chamber could not convict on it, the motion it to be allowed; third, where there is some evidence but it is such that its strength or weakness depends on the view taken of a witness's credibility and reliability and on one possible view of the facts a Trial Chamber could convict on it, the motion will not be allowed; fourth, if the only relevant evidence when viewed as a whole is so incapable of belief that it would not properly support a conviction even when taken at its highest for at Prosecution, a Rule 98 bis for an acquittal will succeed. We recognise the limited scope of a motion for acquittal. As the Trial Chamber in Strugar stated, it involves no evaluation of the guilt of the accused in light of all the evidence in the case to that stage, nor any evaluation of the respective credit of witnesses, or of the strength and weakness or contradictory evidence which is then before the Chamber. However, in making --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In making its determination, the Trial Chamber must make an evaluation of all the evidence on the trial record. In particular, as indicated by the Hadzihasanovic decision, ignoring evidence presented in the Defence in its favour during the Prosecution case would amount to an error at law. Furthermore while Rule 98 bis proceedings will not ordinarily entertain detailed submissions on specific submissions within counts, Trial Chambers have dismissed counts in part, where there is no evidence in support of distinct aspects of a broad charge. In the Strugar decision, for instance, in relation to counts of unlawful shelling of civilian objects, the Chamber dismissed 52 buildings and structures contested by the Defence on the grounds that the evidence did not mention or identify the objects or that the evidence did not establish that the objects were in fact damaged. This is at paragraph 78 of the Strugar 98 bis decision. The partial dismissal of charges is consistent with the object and purpose of Rule 98 bis which is, to quote the Strugar decision: "To separate out and bring to an end those proceedings in respect of a charge for which there is no evidence on which a Trial Chamber could convict. It is consistent with a fundamental principle of justice that a defendant is under no obligation to answer a case that has not been properly made by the Prosecution." In the present case this principle has particular relevance to the unlawful attack charges against General Gotovina as a distinct actus reus of persecution under the umbrella charge of count 1, which is at the core of the Prosecution's JCE theory, as I shall explain. It has relevance also for the multiple murder charges as part of the Count 1, 6, and 7. In view of the distinct prohibited acts that constitute the physical elements of persecution, it is our submission that the Chamber may dismiss Count 1 in part, though it is our view that it should be dismissed as a whole. The Prosecution has advanced two theories of liability. First, it is alleged in paragraph 12 of the indictment that General Gotovina participated in a category 1 JCE, the common purpose being the permanent removal of the Serb population from the Krajina region. The members of this JCE included the highest authorities of the Croatian state, acting jointly in furtherance of a criminal policy. The JCE was allegedly conceived during a meeting on the island of Brioni on 31 July 1995, and implemented through Operation Storm during August 4th and 5th, which consisted allegedly of large-scale indiscriminate artillery attacks intended to terrorise the Serbian civilian population and to force their mass exodus, and which allegedly, in fact, resulted in their massive forcible displacement. In continuation of the same JCE, Operation Storm was allegedly followed by the large-scale destruction and appropriation of Serbian property and other discriminatory measures preventing the displaced population from returning. In addition to these crimes that constitute the purpose of a category 1 JCE, the indictment alleges by way of JCE category 3, that it was foreseeable that the crimes of murder, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment were a possible consequence in the execution of the enterprise. The Prosecution 's alternative theory of liability is that General Gotovina is responsible for crimes committed by his subordinates under the doctrine of command responsibility, under article 7(3). In particular, while it is not contested by the Prosecution that orders were repeatedly issued to respect humanitarian law and that there was a 151 per cent increase in disciplinary measures, and an additionally, that conscripts responsible for crimes were it demobilised, it is still alleged that these did not constitute necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes. There can be no doubt that allegations of large-scale unlawful shelling are at the core of the Prosecution theory against General Gotovina. In Mr. Tieger's opening statement, at pages 418 and 419 of the transcript, he stated as follows: "By the time Operation Storm and its accompanying mop-up operations were over, almost the entire population had been driven out and the Serb community was a scarred wasteland of destroyed villages and homes. By the end of the first day of the operation, the vast majority of Krajina Serbs were in panic stricken flight, not by accident, but by design, through a successfully implemented plan to achieve just that through the shelling of civilian towns and villages. General Gotovina planned an ordered the artillery operation that was intended to drive the Serb civilians out." Further, at page 443, lines 23 to 24 of the transcript, Mr. Tieger once again confirms the Prosecution theory that, and I quote: "The shelling of Knin and other towns was at the core of the plan to drive Serbs out." Accordingly, if the allegation of large-scale unlawful shelling cannot be sustained by the evidence, the Prosecution's entire JCE theory collapses. As we shall set forth in our pleadings today, after a 14-year exhaustive investigation, the Prosecutor has failed to provide any evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the counts set forth in the indictment. First, in relation to persecution under Count 1, there is no evidence whatsoever that Operation Storm was in fact an unlawful discriminatory attack directed not at military objectives but rather directed against the Serbian civilian population. The Prosecution has not produced conclusive evidence of a single unlawful attack or of a single civilian death or injury resulting from such an attack, notwithstanding its burden of proving that unlawful attacks were committed on a widespread or systematic scale as required by Article 5. Second, in relation to deportation and forcible transfer under Counts 1 to 3, because there is no evidence of unlawful attacks against civilians, it follows that there is also no evidence that their displacement resulted from grounds not permitted in international law, as required by Articles 5(d) and (i). Additionally there is no evidence that the shelling, whether unlawful or not, was in fact the cause of civilian flight. There is also no evidence that civilians would have stayed had Croatia captured the Krajina by means other than shelling. The evidence of RSK propaganda and evacuation orders only reinforces the conclusion that there is no causal relationship between shelling and civilian flight, as required by Articles 5(d) and (i). Thus it is our respectful submission that there is simply no evidence whether direct or circumstantial to sustain either the Prosecution's core theory of a JCE at Brioni with the intention of terrorising and expelling civilians on discriminatory grounds or to sustain the Prosecution case that the crimes of persecutory unlawful attacks and deportation were in fact committed irrespective of the existence of the JCE. The evidence simply does not prove either the mens rea or the actus reus of these core crimes. Third, in relation to plunder, wanton destruction, and other discriminatory measures under Counts 1, 4, and 5, without proof of the Brioni JCE to terrorise and expel civilians and in view of undisputed evidence of orders ... JUDE ORIE: Mr. Akhavan, your speed of speech is still a bit high, and although with the text, the interpreters and perhaps the transcriber can catch up, but that's not the way. You should slow down, so that we have a direct and firsthand transcription and translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: My apologies to the Chamber and to the translators. And in view of undisputed evidence of orders to maintain law and order, and notwithstanding evidence that destruction and appropriation of Serbian property was the result of lawlessness in the aftermath of Operation Storm, there is no evidence of an additional JCE with the intention of plundering and destroying property and no evidence that General Gotovina made significant contribution to such crimes. Further more, there is no evidence of a policy to acquiesce in such crimes of mob violence as required by Article 5. Fourth, in relation to murder and inhumane and cruel treatment under counts 6 to 9, without evidence of a category 1 JCE, there is no basis to attribute liability to General Gotovina on the basis of a category 3 JCE. Fifth, in relation to liability, for Counts 1 to 5, based on command responsibility under Article 7(3), there is no evidence to support the Prosecution theory that General Gotovina failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes committed by his subordinates. There is no evidence that beyond repeated orders to respect humanitarian law, disciplinary measures and demobilization of conscripts, none of which is contested by the Prosecution, that General Gotovina had any authority to take additional measures. In particular, there is no evidence that General Gotovina was in command and control of the 72nd Military Police Battalion for the purpose of conducting criminal investigations. Sixth, in relation to liability for Counts 6 to 9, based on command responsibility, there is no evidence that General Gotovina had any notice that beyond plunder and destruction his subordinates were responsible for murder or inhumane and cruel treatment of civilians. I shall now set forth the legal elements required for each of the crimes and the theories of liability as charged by the Prosecution and a corresponding summary as to why the evidence cannot sustain a conviction. In this regard, it is self-evident that under Rule 98 bis, the burden of the Prosecutor is not only to prove all the mental and physical elements of the crimes charged beyond a reasonable doubt, but also to prove the specific theory of liability set forth in its case in chief. The Defence must necessarily rely on the Prosecution theory of the case. It cannot speculate as to hypothetical theories that have not been pleaded in the case in chief. I shall begin by addressing the charge of unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, as a persecutory act under Count 1. As mentioned, this is at the core of the Prosecution theory that General Gotovina participated in the alleged Brioni JCE through Operation Storm and that this combat operation constituted a large-scale persecutory unlawful attack against civilians with the intention to terrorise them into leaving in violation of Article 5(h). The law on JCE provides that General Gotovina must have shared the criminal purpose of an unlawful attack and made a significant contribution to its achievement. In the words of the Brdjanin appeal judgement, and I quote from paragraph 431: "Where all the requirements for JCE liability are met beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused has done far more than merely associate with criminal persons. He has the intent to commit a crime; he has joined with others to achieve this goal; and he has made a significant contribution to the crime's commission." Further more, as the Krajisnik appeals judgement recently confirmed the mens rea for first category JCE is that, and I quote from paragraph 200: "The JCE participants including the accused had a common state of mind; namely, the state of mind that the statutory crimes forming part of the objective should be carried out. In other words, there must be evidence that there was a common criminal purpose to terrorise civilians, specifically through unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects and that General Gotovina joined with others to achieve this goal. The Prosecution contends that this evidence is found in the Brioni transcript. As my colleague Mr. Kehoe will explain, the portions of the Brioni transcript that the Prosecution relies on to impute a JCE to attack Serb civilians when read in context is, at best, highly ambiguous, if not contrary to the Prosecution theory. There is simply no direct evidence of a criminal purpose. The existence of a JCE must be and is in fact circumstantially inferred by the Prosecution from the actual conduct of Operation Storm. The question, therefore, is what circumstances would allow for such an inference to be made as a matter of evidence? In determining what are the conduct of hostilities during Operation Storm constituted a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population as required by Article 5, the Kunarac appeals judgement has head, and I quote: "The laws of war provide a benchmark against which the Chamber may assess the nature of the attack and the legality of the acts committed in its midst." Thus, if there is no evidence that the combat operations violated the laws of war on a large-scale, a conviction under Article 5 cannot be sustained with respect to Operation Storm. In this regard, we note that during the Rule 72 proceedings on jurisdiction, the Prosecution vigorously argued that the laws of war on conduct of hostilities, the so-called Hague law, do not apply to Article 5 charges. The Prosecution subsequently added distinct allegations of unlawful attacks as a persecutory act, first, in its pre-trial brief, and subsequently in the amended indictment under Count 1, and has in substance invoked the terms of additional protocol I of 1977 throughout its case in chief. As you will be well aware from the landmark Galic case, Mr. President, the Prosecution in that case submitted and the Trial Chamber accepted that, and I quote from paragraph 144: "When considering the general requirements of Article 5, the body of laws of war plays an important part in the assessment of the legality of the acts committed in the course of an armed conflict and whether the population may be said to have been targeted as such." The Prosecution has alleged that the provisions of protocol I have been violated on a large-scale within the scope of Article 5. With respect to unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects under Count 1, the Galic case provides a useful statement of the applicable laws of war on protection of the civilian population under Article 51 of additional protocol I, that I will now turn to briefly. In that judgement, the Trial Chamber held at paragraph 56 that the crime of attack on civilians requires the following specific elements, and I quote: "First, acts of violence directed against the civilian population or individual civilians not taking direct part in hostilities causing death or serious injury to body or health within civilian population. Second, the offender wilfully made the civilian population or individual civilians not taking direct part in hostilities the object of those acts of violence." The Trial Chamber goes on to state at paragraph 57 that indiscriminate attacks, that is to say, attacks which strike civilians or civilian objects and military objectives without distinction may qualify as direct attacks against civilians. Thus, the mens rea required for the two categories is closely related. With respect to the mens rea of a disproportionate attack, the Trial Chamber held at paragraph 59, that the Prosecution must prove that the attack was launched wilfully and in knowledge of circumstances giving rise to the expectation of excessive civilian casualties. Since the core Prosecution theory is that Operation Storm was intended to terrorise the civilian population through the unlawful use of artillery, it may also be useful to briefly consider the law applicable to the crime of spreading terror against civilians under Article 51(2) of Protocol I. Although it has not been charged or referred to by the Prosecution, it provides guidance as to how to assess allegations that Operation Storm was intended to terrorise civilians. In explaining the context of combat operations within which the laws of war are meant to apply, the ICRC commentary to Protocol I at paragraph 1940 points out, and I quote: "There is no doubt that acts of violence related to a state of war almost always give rise to some degree of terror among the population and sometimes also among the armed forces. It also happens that attacks on armed forces are purposely conducted brutally, in order to intimidate the enemy soldiers and persuade them to surrender. This is not the sort of terror envisaged here. This provision is intended to prohibit acts of violence, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population without offering substantial military advantage." I will not burden the Trial Chamber with a discussion of what constitutes military advantage, as defined in Article 52(2) of Protocol I or the long list of what constitutes military objective as articulated others of the international Red Cross and various national manuals on the laws of war. But against the exacting standard that I have just set forth on proof of what constitutes unlawful attack, what is the evidence on record that can sustain a conviction that General Gotovina shared a criminal common purpose to terrorise and deport an entire civilian population through large-scale unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects and that such crimes were in fact committed. With the greatest respect to the Prosecution, we submit that there is nothing in the record, nothing whatsoever, that could either allow for an inference that there was a Brioni JCE to commit unlawful attacks or to prove that such acts ever occurred. The Prosecution case at its highest proves only that Croatian forces engaged in artillery attacks against Knin and other locations. Target lists and witness testimony indicate that these locations all contained multiple military objectives. There is no evidence whatsoever of any attacks directed at civilians. The Prosecution has not submitted a single crater analysis on a weapon fired by the Croatian forces. Moreover, the Prosecution has not submitted any evidence whatsoever of disproportionate civilian casualties or damage resulting from artillery fire against Knin or any other town in the so-called Krajina. In fact, it has not even been proven that there was a single civilian death or injury that resulted from an unlawful attack. The evidence that, in addition to artillery, multiple-barrel rocket launchers or MBRLs were used in combat does not prove an unlawful attack either. There is it no evidence whatsoever that MBRLs were in fact not directed or not capable of being directed against specific military objectives. And there is no evidence whatsoever, that in fact they caused unlawful death or injury to civilians or unlawful damage to civilian objects. No evidence whatsoever. It is evidence that in building its case, the Prosecution has applied the wrong standard in alleging unlawful attacks. In particular, we point to Mr. Russo's question to Marko Rajcic at page 16284 [Realtime transcript read in error "12684"] of the transcript, lines 12 to 14, where he asked the following question, and I quote: "Q. Were the 130-millimetre guns and 122-millimetre rocket systems, were they capable of being fired at those targets and only hitting those targets and nothing else around them?" This remarkable question assumes that there must be a 100 per cent rate of accuracy in the use of weapon systems. It completely disregards the Protocol I standards that permit incidental casualties and damage, provided that it is not excessive in relation to the military advantage gained. By Mr. Russo's fastidious standards, every combat operation in the world would constitute a war crime, because there is always a margin of error, even for the sophisticated and precise weapon systems of the world's most advanced armies. Indeed there is considerable evidence that Operation Storm was in fact executed with exceptional military precision and effect. As Mr. Kehoe will explain, the only evidence the Trial Chamber has been presented on collateral damage from shelling, including UNMO and UNCIVPOL reports, demonstrates in fact that the damage was minimal for an operation of this large-scale and that the damage was concentrated around military objectives. For example, we refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibits P64, P228, D66, and D276.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We submit that vague or speculative evidence that artillery was fired in what appears from a distance to be a civilian area is not conclusive proof that an attack was unlawful. You will be well aware, Mr. President, of the exacting evidentiary standards that were applied in this regard in the Galic case, to give but one example. In that case, the majority concluded that a large-scale unlawful attack was proven based on detailed investigation and testimony of numerous incidents of sniping and shelling. The judgement refers, for instance, to evidence that civilians were targeted during funerals, in ambulances, in hospitals, on trams, on buses, when driving or cycling. Against this standard there is no evidence whatsoever of a single unlawful attack, let alone widespread or systematic attacks, wilfully directed against civilians. The Prosecution case, taken at its highest, could not even satisfy a probable cause test, let alone proof beyond a reasonable doubt. We submit, therefore, that the charge of unlawful attack against civilians and civilian objects as an element of persecution under Count 1 be dismissed in its entirety. Furthermore, since this allegation is at the core of the Prosecution's Brioni JCE theory, the entire JCE theory fails. As I shall now explain because the deportation and forcible transfer charges under Counts 1 to 3 depend on proof that Operation Storm was unlawful, they also fail. Based on the standards set forth in the Stakic appeals judgement at paragraph 278: In order to sustain a conviction on deportation or forcible transfer under Articles 5(d) and (i), the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the intention underlying Operation Storm was, and I quote: "The forced displacement of persons by expulsion or other forms of coercion without grounds permitted under international law." Since there is no evidence of an unlawful attack, this charge must also fail. If there is no unlawful attack, there is no forced displacement without grounds permitted under international law. If the flight of civilians from war zones ipso facto constituted deportation, then lawfully combat would be impossible. Count 1 in relevant part and Counts 2 and 3 in whole must be dismissed for this reason alone. There are, however, additional reasons why these counts fail. The Prosecution has not provided any evidence that civilians in fact fled because of shelling, whether lawful or not, although this is at the core of its theory. To the contrary, the evidence indicates that civilians left pursuant to RSK evacuation orders. There is also no evidence that civilians would have remained had Croatian forces captured Krajina through other means. Once again, the evidence demonstrates to the contrary, that the RSK propaganda had instilled the view that Serbs could never live under Croatian state. There is yet a further reason in law why a conviction on these counts cannot be sustained. As the Stakic trial judgement has held at paragraph 674, deportation or forcible transfer is, and I quote: "The removal of someone from the territory over which the person removing exercises sovereign authority." The Krnojelac trial judgement further confirms that the requirement of occupation under Article 49 of the 4th Geneva Convention of 1949 applies equally to deportation charges under Article 5 of the statute. I refer the Chamber to the judgement at paragraph 473, which states that the contents of the underlying offence does not defer whether perpetrated as a war crime or as a crime against humanity. It is it our submission, therefore, that the evidence cannot sustain a conviction under Count 1 in relevant part and Counts 2 and 3 as a whole. There is no basis for a circumstantial inference of an intent to deport, and there is in fact no proof of the actus reus of forced displacement contrary to international law. The Prosecution case is that the fundamental purpose of the alleged Brioni JCE is unlawful shelling to achieve mass expulsion. Without any proof of these two vital elements, it is difficult to see how this JCE theory can be salvaged. The lack of proof that Operation Storm was unlawful also demonstrates that there is no proof of discriminatory intention which is required to sustain a conviction on Count 1 as a whole. Based on the Stakic appeals judgement, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that General Gotovina acted with the intent to commit the underlying act and the intent to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Appeals Chamber has further specified at paragraph 737 that discriminatory intent, the discriminatory intent requirement amounts to a dolus specialis. This is it the highest degree of mens rea in international criminal law. The Kupreskic trial judgment notes at paragraph 636 that the mens rea requirement for persecution is higher than for ordinary crimes against humanity. And at paragraph 751, that persecution is only one step away from genocide. This exacting mental element means that beyond mere knowledge of a discriminatory policy, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that General Gotovina had the conscious desire to discriminate against Serb civilians, merely because of their ethnicity. The Stakic appeals judgement makes it clear at paragraph 329 that: "This discriminatory intent can be neither presumed nor transferred from the direct perpetrators. Therefore, it is immaterial for the assessment of the intent of the indirect perpetrator, whether or not the actor had such a discriminatory intent." It is not sufficient to argue, as the Prosecution did at some length, that because President Tudjman allegedly had discriminatory intention, that General Gotovina also acted with the same special intention. There is no evidence on record whatsoever that proofs discriminatory intention on the part of General Gotovina and for that reason, a conviction for the charge of persecution cannot be sustained, and Count 1 should be dismissed as a whole. Since there is no evidence to support the Prosecution core theory of a JCE, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt with respect to plunder and wanton destruction that there is was a specific JCE in relation to Counts 4 and 5, and Count 1 in relevant part, to commit those specific acts. There is no evidence that a plan of systematic burning or looting was ever complicated at Brioni. As Mr. Kehoe will describe, the Prosecution does not contest that there was series of high level meetings prior to Operation Storm, at which the most senior Croatian state officials made a plan to maintain law and order in Krajina post-liberation and issued orders to the military and civilian police consistent with this objective. In particular, as Mr. Misetic will explain, it is not in dispute that General Gotovina issued attack orders requiring compliance with the Geneva Conventions, that he issued additional orders requiring maximum respect in the treatment of civilians, and as admitted by Prosecution expert Theunens, there was a 151 per cent increase in disciplinary actions within the Split Military District at the relevant time. It is also not contested that General Gotovina demobilised undisciplined conscripts and that he did not receive reports after August 18th that these measures not been effective with respect to his subordinates. The Prosecution case is merely that the Croatian state and General Gotovina did not take adequate measures and thereby infers a discriminatory policy to acquiesce in such crimes against civilian property. While there is no legal requirement of a policy, the Kupreskic trial judgment indicates at paragraph 552 that need for crimes against humanity to have been at least tolerated by a state, government, or entity is stressed in national and international case law. Article 72(A) of the ICC statute in fact requires that the acts be committed pursuant to or in furtherance of a state or organisational policy. At the very least, the mere fact that crimes are numerous does not qualify as crimes against humanity, if there is no proof of a policy of acquiescence. In particular, mob violence in the context of what several witnesses described as lawlessness in the Krajina does not meet either the high threshold or the object and purpose of Article 5. The Tadic trial judgement at paragraph 653 explained that the reason why crimes against humanity so shock the conscience is because they are not isolated random acts of individuals. The cumulative commission of isolated or random crimes by individuals or small groups, thus, is not a crime against humanity. The Prosecution case at its highest proofs that the Croatian state should have tried harder. That it should have allocated more resources to prevent crimes, as tens of thousands of displaced persons returned to their homes in this vast and remote region. There is no evidence, however, as to whether such resources were in fact available. At best, the Prosecution has made the case that Croatia, as with NATO forces in Kosovo, may have been negligent in planning the post-combat requirements of maintaining law and order. It has not proved that there was a deliberate policy of acquiescence as required by Article 5. In this respect, the Prosecution cannot simply allege that there was at Brioni a joint criminal enterprise to commit burning and looting. The Krajisnik appeals judgement has recently held that there cannot be a fluid JCE concept such that beyond the original crimes envisaged allegedly at Brioni that expanded crimes can be attributed to the defendant without additional evidence. The Prosecution cannot merely allegation that there was a broad JCE to commit ethnic cleansing and that the crimes irresistibly evolved from unlawful shelling to burning and looting. The Prosecution must provide specific evidence as required by the Krajisnik appeals judgement, as to whether the JCE members did nothing to prevent the recurrence and persisted in the implementation of this expansion of the common objective and evidence. And furthermore, there must be specific evidence as to when the expanded crimes became incorporated into the common objective. That's at paragraph 171. Since there is no evidence of a JCE to terrorise and expel the Serbian civilian population through unlawful shelling, and since there is also no evidence of a specific or additional JCE to plunder and destroy Serbian property, the JCE theory, as a whole, cannot be sustained, including with respect to relevant parts of Count 1 and Counts 4 and 5 as a whole. Furthermore, since a category 1 JCE has not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt, there can be no category 3 liability with respect to murder and inhumane and cruel treatment under Counts 6 to 9. We submit, therefore, that all of the Counts in the indictment be dismissed to the extent that they are based on JCE liability. Finally, Mr. President, I shall discuss the only remaining basis for liability, which is command responsibility under Article 7(3). As set forth previously and as Mr. Misetic will explain in greater detail, General Gotovina took a number of disciplinary and preventative measures. The Prosecution theory under Article 7(3) rests essentially on the allegation that these measures did not constitute necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes, that General Gotovina should have tried harder. The Prosecution pre-trial brief at paragraph 67 specifically alleges that necessary and reasonable measures that could have been taken by Gotovina include investigating the allegation using military police, notifying appropriate military and civilian prosecution authorities, and imposing immediately disciplinary measures or disciplinary sentences on suspected subordinates to prevent further crimes. As my colleague Mr. Misetic will explain, beyond these allegations the Prosecution has not provided any evidence as to what constitutes necessary and reasonable measures for an operational commander with General Gotovina's responsibilities. And as the Prosecution admits in the pre-trial brief, General Gotovina was in charge of 130.000 soldiers during Operation Storm. We also note that the Prosecution chose not to call Andrew Pringle who was listed as the Prosecution expert witness on command responsibility. The Halilovic trial judgement indicates that whether necessary and reasonable measures are in fact taken is determined by -- had this is at paragraph 74 whether specific orders prohibiting or stopping the criminal activities were issued, what measures to secure the implementation of these orders were taken, what other measures were taken to ensure that the unlawful acts were interrupted, and after the commission of the crime what steps were taken to secure an adequate investigation and to bring the perpetrators to justice. The Prosecution does not deny that General Gotovina issued orders and took disciplinary measures. Instead, it focuses on the failure to investigate crimes. In this respect, the Hadzihasanovic trial judgement indicates at paragraph 1061 that: "Referring the matter to the appropriate military judicial authority is a necessary and reasonable measure, where a commander is unable to carry out his own criminal investigation." As Mr. Misetic will explain, there is no evidence that General Gotovina failed to refer crimes to the military police. There is no evidence that criminal investigation was in fact within the competence of General Gotovina. The Blaskic appeals judgement indicates, at paragraph 72 that: "... necessary and reasonable measures are such that can be taken within the competence of a commander, as evidenced by the degree of effective control he wielded over his subordinates." In this respect, the Prosecution evidence, taken at its highest, merely proves that General Gotovina had general rights of intervention with respect to the military police. The Halilovic appeals judgement expressly states that this is it not a sufficient basis for attribution of command responsibility. In that case, the Appeals Chamber citing the famous high command case before the United States Military Tribunal, held as follows - this is at paragraph 212: "As a commander in chief of an army group, the duties imposed upon Field Marshal von Leeb were exclusively operational, and his headquarters and staff were strictly operational in their functions. Therefore, his authority in the field of executive power was more in the nature of a right to intervene than a direct responsibility." The Military Tribunal found that under the circumstances of the case, it was not considered that criminal responsibility attached to him merely on the theory of subordination and overall command. Considering the acquittal in this regard of Field Marshal von Leeb in the high command case, despite the evidence of massive atrocities of Nazi forces in occupied territories, it would be inconceivable to hold General Gotovina liable under Article 7(3) merely because he allegedly had general rights of intervention with respect to the military police. We submit, therefore, that there is no evidence that could sustain a conviction based on Article 7(3) and, therefore, that all Counts should be dismissed by the Trial Chamber. In summary, Mr. President, distinguished members of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecutor has failed to present proof beyond a reasonable doubt of General Gotovina's criminal liability on any of the counts in the joinder indictment. Accordingly, we respectfully request this Trial Chamber to enter a judgement of acquittal on all Counts. That concludes my submissions. I thank you for your attention and ask the Chamber to give the floor to my colleague Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. And Your Honours, good morning. I would like to continue to expand on the discussion as presented by Mr. Akhavan, directing my comments for the most part to the JCE allegations. In substance, again as outlined by Mr. Akhavan, the JCE allegation involving General Gotovina is that there was a plan to drive the Serb civilian population out of the Krajina, that that plan was concretized at the meeting in Brioni, that General Gotovina shared in this criminal purpose, and that his significant contribution came through the use of artillery during Operation Storm. I will attempt to lay out the evidence in this fashion without commenting, of course, on credibility, et cetera, Your Honour as I know is not proper, and trying to look at the evidence from the Prosecution but in all -- all of the evidence. And in doing so, one must reflect on the whole body of evidence that the Prosecution has made this allegation concerning the JCE, and face -- in the face of several salient facts; the first, of course, being that the liberation of the Krajina had been planned by Croatian forces for years. The second was that the plan and use of artillery and rockets on military objectives in Knin and other cities in the -- in the Krajina had been planned well prior to the Brioni meeting. Next, that the Serb population began to leave the Krajina prior to Operation Storm. Also, that in parallel to the planning of Operation Storm, Croatian ministries were preparing for the peaceful reintegration of the Krajina and the restoration of law and order. Lastly, that the shelling was done in support of a military offensive and we will discuss these points. That there was no extensive loss of life and damage to civilian structures in Knin or other locales, as a result of this shelling on 4th and 5th of August. During its opening statement and its pre-trial brief, the Prosecution has stressed the importance of the Brioni meeting and what was discussed. I think -- I submit to the Chamber that it's important before we look at those comments as a -- as pointed out by the Prosecution that we look at the context of Brioni in line with all of the evidence that is before the Chamber. What we know is that prior to Brioni, that there was a plan to re-take the Krajina, and that the plan for use of artillery against Knin and other locales, with specific target it's listed, dated back to at least 1993. We take that from Marko Rajic's statement, D1425, at paragraph 50. What else do we know? We know that as we move further towards the July 31st date, we need to focus on the directive from the HV staff of the 26th of June of 1995, and that is D956. And what do we learn from that directive, more than a month prior to Brioni? What we learn is that the Main Staff directed General Gotovina and the other -- district level commanders that they were to use artillery and rockets against Knin and Benkovac and other locales. And if you are looking at the English of that particular document, it is on page 5. They also note in page 6 of D956, under heading 7, artillery and rocket support, that the support should focus on neutralizing the Republika Srpska army Main Staff, 7 Corps command post in Knin, the brigade command post, concentrations of enemy manpower, et cetera, and the last sentence, preventing an enemy counterattack from the direction of Knin, Kastel Zegarski, and Benkovac. We also know that after the Brioni meeting there was a visit from Ambassador Galbraith to President Tudjman, and we can reference that on trial transcript 4928, line 13, through 4929, line 2. In that conversation, inter alia, Ambassador Galbraith states to President Tudjman that the Serb population will have to be protected, that prisoners of war will be treated well -- well treated, excuse me, that any atrocities would affect US/Croat relations and that the safety of the UN peacekeepers was paramount. On that same date, again from Marko Rajcic, at D425 at paragraph 9, in a meeting with General Gotovina, General Gotovina emphasised that the purpose of this endeavour was to obtain a military victory and the operation was aimed only against the enemy soldiers. Now, one would expect that if there was there significant meeting taking place on the 31st of July at Brioni, that there would be in fact dramatic changes in orders given by Military District commanders, such as General Gotovina, in furtherance of the shelling of the civilian population, to drive the civilian population out of Knin. What we see is something, of course, quite different. And I direct Your Honour's attention to a document that I'm sure Your Honours have seen many times and probably tire of, P1125, which is the Kozjak order of 2 August 1995. There were in fact two additional cities that were due to be attacked and two additional from the first order of the 26th of June that came from the Main Staff, those two cities being Obrovac and Gracac. But now, significantly, the first city on that list is Drvar. Drvar is to be put under artillery fire as the other towns are. What is the significance of Drvar? Drvar is a town that is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not in the Krajina or in the Republic of Croatia. And why was that done? What was the military purpose? Of course, there was a military purpose because the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS was located in that area and, of course, General Gotovina had to protect his flank as they moved into the Knin area and the rest of the Krajina. One would also expect that if this was an artillery operation directed against the civilian population, that it would be a significant bombardment of the civilian population with as much artillery as the HV could muster. Unfortunately, the facts counter that. While the initial order coming from the Main Staff on the 26th of June allowed for six combat sets, the order presented on the 2nd of August by General Gotovina reduced that allotment to in fact four combat sets. So on the heels of Operation Storm, in fact, General Gotovina ordered that less -- excuse me, on the heels of Brioni and prior to Operation Storm, General Gotovina ordered that less artillery be used. Now, the Prosecution has argued in their pre-trial brief, opening statement, and certainly through the evidence that there is -- there was this agreement in Brioni to expel the Serbs from Krajina, and in the case of General Gotovina, through the use of artillery. Now let us look, if we may, at the references that have been presented to the Chamber by the Office of the Prosecutor to support that position. Because after the entire Prosecutor's case, those references are quite revealing. The first one is presented by Mr. Tieger on page 425 of the transcript. This is lines 9 through 11, Mr. Tieger highlighted these comments by General Gotovina: "If there is an order to strike at Knin, we will destroy it in its entirety in a few hours." Now what was the significance of that reference? It becomes, in juncture, somewhat perplexing because of course we know that Knin wasn't destroyed. And in fact on page 444 of the transcript, the Prosecutor acknowledges as much on lines 13 and 14. The next highlighted portion was on page 426, lines 20 to 24. And there is some disagreement, Mr. President and Your Honours, concerning a translation about this particular comment, and the Defence has offered a different translation, minor, in D960. He notes quoting General Gotovina according to the Prosecutor's transcript: "At this moment we can engage in extremely precise operations at Knin systematically without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located." And it said, "the moment all of our weapons are guided, directly guided." Our translation that we submitted is a tad different. It notes that, "at this moment we can engage in extremely precise operations in a planned manner without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located." Suffice it to say, that under either translation, we are talking about the careful, precise, and planned use of artillery. We also know, to contextualise this reference is that in that same document, P461, in pages 21 to 22, General Zagorec who was the logistics officer at this meeting expressed concern about their ammunition levels. And he notes: "I am now only interested in this. And I urge all commanders to take into account the amount of ammunition expended in these operations. We have reserves for some five days." So looking at these comments, we have an assessment from the chief of logistics, that there is limited ammunition with the comment by General Gotovina that the artillery fire can be careful, precise, and in a planned manner. The last comment referencing General Gotovina by the Prosecutor came on page 426 -- excuse me, page 426 of the Prosecutor's opening. And it was cited in this fashion - now, mind you, this is it comment on the 31st of July, 1995, Pre-storm. In lines 4, "that means if we continue this pressure, probably for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving." Now, the Prosecutor has opined that this refers to artillery. But let us harken back to one very significant point at this juncture and that is prior to the 4th of August, 1995 the HV never shelled Knin and never shelled the -- most of the other cities that have been brought before this Chamber. I do believe there was some testimony that there was some intermittent shelling in Benkovac in 1993 and 1994, but clearly the evidence is that Knin had never bee so shelled. So given the fact that prior to 31st July there had been no shelling, and that we had seen significant HV advances in winter 1994 jump one and jump 2 in June 1995, and the takeover of Glamoc and Bosanski Grahovo in July of 1995, ending in approximately the 28th of July, clearly this is the pressure to which the parties are alluding, not pressure coming from artillery that had yet to take place. Lastly, the comment that the Serbs would be leaving in reference to, there won't be so many civilians, it was well recognised, number one, that the Serb population certainly after the fall of Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc had been leaving. But, number two, from the Prosecutor's own witness Ambassador Peter Galbraith that should sectors north and south fall that the Krajina Serbs would leave. I refer Your Honours to Ambassador Galbraith's diary that the Prosecutor put into evidence, P459. And I quote by Ambassador Galbraith: "If Croatia took the territory," and contextually he is referring to Sectors North and South, "the Krajina Serbs would leave. They could be resettled in Sector East, thus threatening Milosevic's claim to territory that he very much wants for Greater Serbia." Well, if that doesn't prove anything, if that doesn't prove anything -- by the way I just reminded, that entry by Ambassador Galbraith was on June 15th of 1995. Let us turn to -- if that doesn't establish anything, let's turn to the comments by President Tudjman that have also been cited by the Prosecution. And frankly, when we look at the first one, even the Prosecutor, at page 424, noted that the comments by President Tudjman were somewhat ambiguous. This is in the transcript, at pages 423 and 424, it's a quoting of President Tudjman, starting on line 3: "In which way do we resolve it? That is the subject of our discussion today. We have to inflict such blows that the Serbs will, to all practical purposes, disappear, that is to say, the areas that we do not take at once must be -- must capitulate within a few days. Therefore our main task is not Bihac, but to inflict such blows in several directions that the Serbian forces will no longer be able to recover but will have to capitulate." Now, quite clearly, from the words of President Tudjman he is referring to an attack to defeat the Serbian forces. Plain and simple. The next comment often used by the Prosecutor is again a comment by President Tudjman at page 424 and 425, and I am giving the full context, not reading all of it. But his comments are instructive at the beginning, where he says: "Gentlemen, I accept your views in principle. There is still something missing, and that is the fact that in such a situation when we undertake a general offensive in the ... area, even grater panic will break out in Knin than has to date." Even greater panic. Quite clearly the reference is panic that is existing in Knin on the 31st of July that came as a result of the offensive operations of the HV throughout the summer, or actually going back to the winter of 1994, and the summer of 1995. Now, certainly if you go back to the comments made by my learned friend, Mr. Akhavan, will there be additional panic as a result of another military offensive? Of course. I don't think anybody would dispute that. But the reference is not panic because of the use of artillery. The reference is because of the overall situation. So let us look at these comments and let's look at this Brioni transcript as the basis for this JCE meeting of the minds. Quite clearly, looking at this in isolation -- at this meeting, there was no meeting; there was no agreement; there was no agreement to participate in some time of criminal endeavour. There was no proof, based on this agreement, that the Prosecutor has put so much stock in that there was in fact a JCE. The Prosecutor says, well, let's look at the actual conduct of the operations. Let's look at how Operation Storm unfolded, because certainly from that we can extrapolate an intent to participate in this JCE, wherever it was formed which is now somewhat amorphous and problematic vis-a-vis Krajisnik. But nevertheless, let us take this endeavour and look at this matter in a light most favourable to the Prosecutor because I believe that even under those circumstances, I submit to the Chamber that there is no evidence of a JCE; there's no evidence of an any significant participation in any alleged JCE, because the attack on the Krajina on the 4th and the 5th of August, 1995, was legal from the beginning to the end and lawful. Let's look at some of the issues raised by the Prosecutor because at this juncture, Mr. President, Your Honours, Your Honours has to look at the full body of evidence and at the Prosecutor's case, and we acknowledge that. One document that they have put a tremendous amount of stock in is the Kozjak order. Again I reference that, P1124, page 14, where they have quoted on numerous occasions putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire. What does that establish? Well, again, we have to contextualise the entire sentence in many fashions, not only looking at the document itself and that paragraph in toto but also now contextualise it with the rest of the evidence, i.e., the individual who wrote it, being Marko Rajcic, an individual who came before the Court. Quite clearly when we look at this document it has the commander as intent as a preface, and I quote: "Tasks of artillery rocket groups, groups and organised TS and TRS-2 along many attack axes focus on providing artillery support to the main forces in the offensive operation through powerful strikes against the enemy front line command posts, communications, centres, artillery firing positions, and also the other towns that we just referenced. When Mr. Rajcic was brought before the Chamber, he was not asked about that particular portion of the document, so the Gotovina Defence asked. And I turn to put this entire matter in context, and I reference page 16535, line 7, through 16536, line 6. And I will focus first on lines 19 to 23 of 16535. And he was asked, after stating that he in fact wrote this portion of the order: "Q. Was the intend of this line in the order to fire at pre-planned military objectives; or was it to just to fire indiscriminately throughout the town? What was it? "A. I never heard nor ever issued an order to the effect to execute indiscriminate fire." Paragraph 24 -- excuse me. Line 24 on 16535: "The other part of my question was, so was the intent of this order to fire on pre-planned military objectives that you -- that you had discussed and planned prior to ... Storm. "I'm sorry, I apologise. It was always implied, understood as far as I was concerned. In other words, it was mandatory for me that exclusively and only a target, a target with specific coordinates. I always maintain that is so, and that this is understood. And that is why I do not always explain ... at length." Interestingly, this particular language that is set forth in the Kozjak order and then in Mr. Rajcic's actually artillery attachment to 1125 doesn't contain this language. And only went out -- to a relatively few group of people. But what do we get from this language that the Prosecutor has put so much stock in? Number one, there is it nothing about targeting civilians; number two, there is nothing about targeting in a way to create panic with the civilian population; and number three, there's nothing about expending scarce military resources on non-military targets. Frankly, it is to the contrary. But the Prosecutor has also presented the argument that the attack on the 4th and 5th of August was in fact directed against the civilian population. That these conductive hostilities constituted a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population. As Your Honours know, and Your Honour, I appreciate your background in the Galic case, the determination of a violation under Article 5 has to be dictated by the laws of war and whether or not the accused violated the laws of war under Article 3 as a subset to Article 5. There has not been any evidence presented by the Prosecution that there was a single unlawful attack that took place in Operation Storm, let alone a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population. Not a single unlawful attack. And I'm not here to say, Mr. President, Your Honours, that during the course of this combat that rounds might have gone into a civilian locale. That does not make a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population. What we do know and that the Prosecution has been unable to overcome is that this attack was in compliance with Article 51 of Protocol I. There is no evidence that the civilian population was made the object of the attack. To the contrary. The evidence that has been presented to this Chamber during the Prosecution's case is that the civilians were not targeted, and that when the HV was planning the artillery operation, that the HV attempted to minimise civilian casualties. Where do we find that? Most easily we find that in the statement of Mr. Rajcic at D1425, paragraph 17. One could make a case, Mr. President, Your Honours, of an attack where the object is the civilian population if one had evidence such as a crater analysis as we saw -- I know Your Honour saw quite routinely in Galic. No such crater analysis took place. We have one crater analysis that the Prosecutor has presented through Mr. Anttila, and that's at transcript page 2686, line 19, and through 2689, line 9. But quite clearly it appears that the expended round that they took was in fact a Serbian round. And Your Honours can review this yet further in the exhibits we presented, D80, D81, D82, D166, and D167. But let's assume for the sake of argument here that the round or the shell casing that was found by Mr. Anttila was in fact fired by the HV, as opposed to the Serbian forces. That single event does not prove or establish in any way that the civilian population was the object of this attack. The next argument that has been presented by the Prosecution, and this came through Colonel Konings and Mr. Rajcic, was the actual challenge to the weapon systems that were employed. And we have heard a lot of evidence about this, and if we just address ourselves to the weapon systems that we used against Knin, we're talking about T130s and 122-millimetre multi-barrel rocket launchers. And the argument seems to go that these weapons, especially the multi-barrel rocket launchers, are incapable of distinguishing between military and civilian targets. Well, I submit to Your Honours that that is not what is contemplated by the principle of distinction as set forth in Article 51. What is -- what is contemplated by Article 51's principle of distinction is the use of things such as chemical weapon or incendiary devices. Or for that matter, if we can get something that we may know quite an about, SCUD missiles that were fired by the Iraqis that had a margin of error of approximately 6 to 10 kilometres, not a weapon system such as employed during Operation Storm. My learned colleague Mr. Akhavan addressed the comment made by Mr. Russo concerning whether or not these weapon systems it be the T130 or a multi-barrel rocket launcher can be fired with the guarantee that it would hit this target and nothing else. At the risk of moving towards hyperbole, Mr. President, Your Honours, a handgun doesn't have that type of accuracy. Certainly over any given distance, it simply does not; it breaks down. And there is no prohibition in international law such as with incendiary and chemical weapons, there is no prohibition in international law or customary law from using these types of weapons systems. Now the question presents itself, can these weapons systems be directed at military objectives as required by Article 51? Well, we know from the initial directive coming on the 26th of June, 1995, that the HV Main Staff concluded that they could. And we know from Mr. Rajcic's statement, again paragraph 16, at D1425, that these weapons were chosen because they were capable of being directed and hitting military objectives. But more importantly, the Prosecutor's expert Lieutenant Konings at page 14758, lines 11 through 15, testified that these weapons could be directed against military targets. And that being the case, the use of this weaponry does not violate the principle of distinction . Now, the other possible way armies, military forces can violate Article 51 certainly is the proportionality equation when looking at the, if we can just quote it quite quickly, in Article 51, the subdivision 5(B) the attack may be expected to cause incidental loss of life, injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects, or a combination thereof, which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Now let us look at this item or this aspect of the law vis-a-vis the evidence. What we know from Mr. Rajcic's testimony is that the attack on the locales in Knin offered a significant military advantage to the HV by knocking out the headquarters, knocking out communications, neutralizing the 7th Krajina Corps or Knin Corps, excuse me, and in doing so, not only bringing an end to the war in Sector South but also bringing an end to Operation Storm and Sector North, an effort that was remarkably successful and brought about a quick capitulation by the ARSK. In looking at the proportionality equation, and I understand, Mr. President, Your Honours, that we are looking after the fact, and that in the instance of following the laws of war, you look at it from the standpoint of the reasonable commander. Nevertheless, the fallout from such a campaign is instructive in determining whether or not this particular commander, in this instance, General Gotovina, failed in his obligations to assess the proportional damage in light of the -- of the military advantage. What we know from the evidence is that there was no disproportionate damage. We know that there was no disproportionate damage from any specific weapon against any specific target. How do we know that? We need only look at the assessments referred to by Mr. Akhavan, by UN, UNCIVPOL, and a multitude of other individuals who were there that are reflected in P64, P228, D66, and D276. Again, when we are looking at proportionality there, it is important to assess exactly what civilians and civilian structures were damaged. And again we have no crater analysis performed on the artillery -- on the artillery that had been fired into Knin on the 4th and the 5th. Equally important is to assess not only damage to structures but more importantly injuries to civilians. How many civilians died as a result of this alleged disproportionate attack? The Prosecutor has been able to establish one. Dr. Clark could only conclude that there was one civilian casualty in Knin consistent with blast injuries, and he couldn't determine if that was a mine, if that was a hand-grenade, if that was an MRL, a T-130. He simply couldn't tell. Equally important, another Prosecution witness Professor Puhovski, and this is at transcript 15971 through 15972, was unable to confirm the excessive civilian casualties as a result of artillery. So what do we have? We have the proper use of weaponry, concentrated on military targets, minimal damage to civilian structures, and one dead civilian, as a result of blast injuries which can't be directly connected to Operation Storm. Based on an analysis of the evidence, quite clearly, there has been no -- this -- this attack had no disproportionate consequences given the military advantages gained by taking the military headquarters, by taking -- by neutralizing communication facilities, and by bringing about the expeditious capitulation by RSK forces. We submit to Your Honours, clearly that under the persecution count, the unlawful attack in that persecution count have not been established at all and have to be dismissed. I hasten to add that they have likewise failed to show that General Gotovina had any discriminatory intent on that score. So persecution would likewise be dismissed for that reason. But going go back to the JCE element, we have established that the shelling was lawful. And contrary to the argument made by the Prosecutor, General Gotovina shared no criminal purpose with anybody else and certainly had no significant contribution to any JCE. Now, if we look back at paragraph 12 of the indictment, it is an attempt to encompass virtually all of these crimes in one lump sum in somewhat of an artful fashion, and I will attempt to parcit through to get through this. But quite clearly it -- General Gotovina is charged with being part of a JCE with a common purpose, among other things, appeared to be the systematic looting and burning. And given the fact that the only meeting that was referenced by the Prosecutor on this score was Brioni, one has to exclude, unless we hear differently and we haven't heard over the past year any differently, that this plan to burn and loot was, again, hatched at Brioni on the 31st of July, 1995. Your Honours, you will search in vain for any such discussion. It doesn't exist. To the contrary we have a remarkable situation, again putting this meeting in Brioni in context, with a variety of other interesting events presented during the course of the Prosecutor's case. I mentioned previously this meeting on 1st August with Ambassador Galbraith. That's referenced on pages 428 and 429, where Ambassador Galbraith tells President Tudjman to safe-guard the civilian population. I'm sorry, 4928, 4929, thank you. It is followed on a meeting on the 2nd of August of 1995 that is reflected in D409 where Minister Susak, General Cervenko, General Gotovina, General Markac, and others, and there are numerous people there, you can see the attendees. But General Susak cautions these individuals that all offences have to be prevented, Military District commanders were who to pass on to other commanders the prohibition of torching and looting, and they must prevent having the heros of the home land war being brought to a Court. Later on that same day in the afternoon, 1730, a similar meeting takes place where Minister Susak and Minister Jarnjak are with Mr. Lausic and Mr. Moric again planning for the -- what's going to happen law and order-wise once the Krajina is taken over. I will note that General Gotovina is not at that meeting. We have yet another meeting on the 3rd where Moric and Lausic are having yet more plans for this matter. We have General Gotovina on the 2nd of August after his meeting with Susak, et cetera, giving an order that there is to be no looting and burning and torching. And that's at D201 which is part of P1125. I might hasten to add when I showed that particular document to Ambassador Galbraith, he noted that this was the kind of document that he was looking for to be passed down by someone like General Gotovina during Operation Storm. That reference is at page 5035, lines 1 through 4. So when we look at the allegations made by the Prosecution from -- from Brioni, we also have to look at a series of orders being given by the highest levels of the Croatian government to protect the civilian population, to stop looting and burning, to set up law and order, and all of those orders have been given out at the highest levels certainly by Minister Susak and Minister Jarnjak. And if we were to go along with the position, the untenable position presented by the Prosecution, those orders were being given with the idea that no one would follow them, because that is the only equation under which the position of the Prosecution makes sense. What's interesting is that I asked that particular question to Ambassador Galbraith at page 5079, lines 23 and 25, and we do go back and forth a little bit about this, so I don't want to focus you on that particular line because there is some discussion prior to that. But in essence, I asked Ambassador Galbraith, did Minister Jarnjak and Minister Susak would, they issue orders that President Tudjman did not want followed? The answer was no. Again, coming out of this Brioni meeting or any other meeting, there is simply no agreement to participate in the looting, and burning in the Krajina or that General Gotovina or any proof that General Gotovina made any significant contribution or was complicitous in any such endeavour at all. Let us turn to the other aspect of the JCE, i.e., the destruction that took place in the Krajina after Operation Storm. We're not here to say that there wasn't burning that took place and looting that took place after Operation Storm. You -- the UNMO assessment is reflective -- certainly the last one, there are many of them, has been reflected in P176. But what was clear from an analysis of that document not only through the witnesses but in documents that -- that have been presented by the Gotovina Defence that in fact both Serb and Croat villages were destroyed on occasion and both Serb and Croat villages were not destroyed. We have attempted to chart out this ironic position given the Prosecutor's case in D1327. The Prosecutor says yet further -- and this is in their opening statement at P457, page -- lines 21 to 23, HV soldiers and police continue to loot the in the houses in Knin with the exception of those marked as Croat houses which were conspicuously preserved. That ended up not being true either. If we look at the transcript of UNMO Peter Marti, Un military observer at page 4686, where he talks about the fact that someone is putting Croatian house on this -- on the outside. And he was questioned. He begins and he starts talking about a young female writing that on her house, Croatian house. And at line 13: "Q. Was she an older lady, younger lady? "A. She was quite young, about 30. "Q. But a civilian? "A. Civilian, yes. "Q. And you noted for us in the same page at line 16 that writing 'Croatian house' was not always a guarantee that the house would remain untouched. Was that your experience? "A. Yes. It happened that even houses were torched or partly damaged which at the signal before Croatian property or whatever." Pardon my comment there, but I'm reading it literally. "Q. Sometimes it didn't make a difference. "A. Yes." That was in fact buttressed by the comments of Mr. Boucher at page 14047, line 13, that is where he says: "That is, there was -- they would be put 'don't touch, Hrvatska kuca,' meaning 'Croatian house.' But even then could you see there was -- there was houses that the doors had been broken into." What does the evidence actually reflect? Certainly there is nothing coming out of the Brioni meeting or in any other meeting where some agreement was formulated to allow this conduct to take place. What are we left with? We are left with the comments and assessment by again a Prosecution witness Peter Marti, where he talks, beginning on -- I believe this is actually this his statement at page 415, page 3 and 4, where he notes that the best description of the looting that took place in the Knin area would be shopping without paying. He notes that: "My personal opinion is that they really were civilians," referring to the people that were causing this damage. "My personal opinion is that they really were civilians, maybe some of them have been in the army before. The looting was not ordered by somebody. Because you couldn't see any kind of systematic pattern in it except from the fact that it was more or less total." What we have and from the evidence presented by the Prosecutor is no evidence to tacitly approve this conduct, no evidence that General Gotovina made any significant contribution to a meeting that had such -- such criminal acts as part of his goal. What we do have is evidence that there was a significant power vacuum by the Croatian government once page storm was completed. In fact, they were too successful in moving too quickly in retaking it. The argument simply is in its substance that the Croatian government should have tried harder to bring law and order to the area. That may be a negligent act on behalf of the Croatian government, but it certainly does not rise to criminal conduct on anyone's part, the least of which is General Gotovina. Going back to the Brdjanin elements that are set forth in paragraph 431: An accused has to have an intend to commit a crime. He has to have -- this is in referring to JCE liability. He has to have intent to commit a crime; he has joined with others to achieve this goal; and he has made a significant contribution to the crime's commission. Sufficient it to say there has been no evidence to support the allegations that there was any intent on behalf of General Gotovina to commit a crime, that he joined with others to commit any such crime, that he knowingly an intentionally joined with others to commit such a crime, nor that he made any significant contribution to any crime's commission given the fact that the one thing that he is accused of doing improperly is the artillery attack on Knin which we have concluded was lawful in all respects. The last part this argument is the failure to punish argument or the 7(3) liability.
