utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Picking up where Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Akhavan left off, is the issue of Article 7(3) liability, as well as the issue of responsibility for murders which are two issues that I will be addressing today. We are, of course, as Mr. Akhavan pointed out cognisant to the fact that this not closing argument and that we are arguing here as to whether the Prosecution has presented not any evidence, but rather any evidence that taken at its highest could be the basis for proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Given that it is it our position that there was no -- certainly no evidence of a JCE to commit large-scale burning and looting, or any evidence that General Gotovina had an intention to participate in relation to such a JCE, the only remaining basis for attribution of liability pursuant to the Statute is under Article 7(3). The Prosecution's theory of General Gotovina's command responsibility rests primarily on an allegation of a failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes. The Halilovic trial judgement gives an indication at paragraph 74 or an explanation, I should say, of what might constitute necessary and reasonable measures. And the Halilovic Trial Chamber found reasonable measures could include specific orders prohibiting or stopping the criminal activities, measures taken to secure the implementation of these orders, other measures taken to ensure that unlawful acts are interrupted, and whether these measures were reasonably sufficient in the specific circumstances, and after the commission of the crime what steps were taken to secure an adequate investigation. The Prosecution's case concedes that General Gotovina did take the following measures. Mr. Theunens' report at page 252, he cites that the Croatian army instituted a plan in the weeks before Operation Storm, i should say a program, that would require international humanitarian law training for officers. The Prosecution concedes that in General Gotovina's attack order for Operation Storm, which is at Exhibit D201, that General Gotovina issued specific preventative orders to prevent the commission of crimes and specifically referenced the need that political affairs officers in the army needed to make sure that subordinates were instructed on their obligations under the Geneva Conventions. In the record in the Split Military District diary at P71, page 83, we have oral -- an oral order on the evening of the 4th that Knin must not experience the same fate as Grahovo. Again at P71, page 84, we have another oral order when information came in to General Gotovina's operational command that the 7th Guards Brigade was about to enter Knin. It is recorded that General Gotovina ordered maximum fairness in the treatment of civilians and behaviour towards the UN. And it is noted that this order has been passed to all operative groups and commanders. After the 5th, on the 6th you have seen the command climate that General Gotovina sent on the now famous Knin video of the meeting on the 6th at the fortress in Knin. On that same video General Gotovina issues an oral order requiring that all war booty be properly registered. The next day, Exhibit D981, General Gotovina issues a written order not only requiring the registration of war booty, but he established a committee to inspect the war booty lists and ensure compliance. Based on information coming from the field, General Gotovina issues another order on the 10th of August, which is Exhibit D204, which is issued in the preamble in order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to save human lives, and in the order he prohibits the arbitrary movement of HV members in the liberated areas and orders that commanders take all necessary measures to prevent arson and undisciplined conduct. On the 12th of August, Split Military District Command political affairs branch at Exhibit P918 issues a warning to lower level political affairs officers that they have to be more energetic in preventing criminality, including arson and theft and the killing of livestock. That exhibit is particularly important as it is uncontested by the -- I should say, not only uncontested by the Prosecution, but indeed a Prosecution Exhibit. Because in it the Split Military District political affairs officer references the fact that it is the policy of President Tudjman and Minister Susak that this type of criminal activity must stop. And again in the overall context of whether the Prosecution has submitted sufficient evidence of a JCE to commit burning and looting, we submit that P918 is the only specific evidence offered by the Prosecution as to what the intentions were of two of the named members of the JCE, and certainly is the evidence of what the subordinates of these individuals thought that the policy was of President Tudjman and Minister Susak. After ordering his subordinates to issue disciplinary measures, in order to protect property and lives, it was confirmed by the Prosecution's in-house expert, Mr. Theunens, that the Split Military District issued 151 per cent more disciplinary measures in the third quarter than they had in the first two quarters. The statistics show that the disciplinary measures taken -- and we've had significant debate in the trial which I will not go into again about the distinction between ordering disciplinary measures for disciplinary infractions and requiring criminal prosecution for criminal actions. But in any event, the Split Military District issues numerous disciplinary measures precisely against soldiers who were AWOL, absent without leave, or otherwise absent from their unit which should be directly connected to General Gotovina's order from the 10th of August at D204, which the first measure that General Gotovina issues in order to present the theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to save human lives, the first measure he issued is to prohibit arbitrary movement of HV members. And so the fact that the statistics show a substantial increase in disciplinary measures taken for absence is significant in that regard. With respect to a specific unit, the evidence is in this case, that there was information of one particular commander who was having difficulty implementing the orders to prevent crime. And this is Exhibit D984, relates to a SIS report of the 18th of August, where the Split Military District Command is advised "the 134th Home Guard Brigade are continuously destroying and burning residential buildings because the commander lacks the necessary authority to implement the orders of Operative Group West." The Split Military District Command immediately, on the basis of that order, takes measures to deal with the problematic unit. D985, an order by General Gotovina of the same date, immediately ordering the formation of a commission to inspect the list of war booty of the 134th, and to compare what was listed with what is actually found on the ground. D884 and D885 are orders of the Split Military District Command to dismiss from the 134th all soldiers who are engaging in illegal conduct or disrupting military discipline. As the Trial Chamber will recall in the cross-examination of Mr. Theunens, the result was following this order that 75 per cent of the 134th Home Guards were demobilised which can be seen by comparing D986, which reports 2302 members of the 134th on the 21st of August; with D987, page 19, which reports 581 left, of which less than 200 are active. Importantly, in the assessment of the Prosecution's claim that General Gotovina failed to take necessary and reasonable measures, it is important to note that Mr. Theunens acknowledged at page 12847 that, after the 18th of August, and after this report about the 134th, there are no further reports in the Split Military District diary or any other reports to the Split Military District command which would indicate or would have indicated to the Split Military District Command that any burning or looting by HV units on the territory of the Republic of Croatia was continuing. Accordingly, we submit, the Prosecution has failed to show and failed to submit any evidence that General Gotovina would have known that the measures that he had taken, up to and including the 18th of August, lacked effectiveness. It is also important to note here, that, in addition to General Gotovina's duties, the Prosecution, in its pre-trial brief, at paragraph 107, acknowledges or states that an armed conflict existed and continued between the HV and the ARSK after the conclusion of Operation Storm, through August, through September, and into October, through Operation Southern Sweep. And at paragraph 107 of the pre-trial brief the Prosecution even references the 12 August counteroffensive against General Gotovina's forces in Bosnia, which the Prosecution states was done by the ARSK and not the VRS. And the Prosecution's position in the pre-trial brief is that hostilities between the ARSK and the HV continued till approximately the 15th of October. So in addition to General Gotovina's duties in Bosnia which is part of the Prosecution's case in chief, he was dealing and took necessary and reasonable measures in the area that he had liberated. Thus, Your Honours, the Prosecution's theory of command responsibility in this case is not that General Gotovina failed to take necessary and reasonable measures; but, rather, that he allegedly failed to take enough necessary and reasonable measures. Glaringly absent from the Prosecution's case in chief, however, was any evidence offered by the Prosecution as to what specific measures were available to General Gotovina that he failed to take. In this regard it is important to note the Prosecution tendered -- I should say, the Prosecution filed an expert report by Major-General Andrew Pringle who was supposed to testify on command and control. In the witness summary filed with the Chamber, the OTP stated that General Pringle was going to give expert testimony to the Trial Chamber about command and control issues, and I quote the Prosecution here: "In particular, in relation to the accused Ante Gotovina and Ivan Cermak based on documentation examined by him." At the end of the Prosecution's case, however, OTP chose not to call General Pringle on this critical issue. We submit that this failure is fatal to the Prosecution's case on command responsibility. Furthermore, the Prosecution failed to elicit from any relevant witness who may have been capable of doing so, such as Mr. Theunens or General Lausic, any evidence with respect to what necessary and reasonable measure General Gotovina failed to take. You will recall my debate with Mr. Theunens, Mr. Theunens's assertion about Drvar and General Gotovina imposing military rule in Drvar in Bosnia. We submit, Your Honours, that that clearly cannot be a necessary and reasonable measure. We await to see if that is in fact what the Prosecution contends. However, we believe there is no evidence to support a claim that General Gotovina had the authority to issue or authorise military rule in liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia. The Prosecution in its pre-trial brief at paragraph 67 alleges that General Gotovina could have done three things: Investigated the allegations using military police or others at his disposal; notifying appropriate military and civilian prosecution authorities, such as the military prosecutor's office of the crimes; and imposing immediate disciplinary measures for disciplinary sentences. The Prosecution's evidence taken at its highest as Mr. Akhavan stated is that it was General Lausic through Major Juric who was in control, in command and control of the military police in its crime prevention, crime investigation, and crime processing functions. In the re-direct examination of Mr. Lausic, the Prosecution posed the question, could General Gotovina have issued an order, which we submit, Your Honour, does not get the Prosecution passed the von Leeb case or the Halilovic Appeals Chamber decision as to whether a hypothetical question about a potential right to intervene is sufficient to establish the failure to take necessary and reasonable measures. For the record, the Gotovina Defence disputes the claim that he had such a right to intervene. With respect to the issue of notifying the military and civilian prosecution authorities, there has been no evidence in the record to indicate that General Gotovina had any knowledge of crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you generally to slow down because I see that there are problems with the French translation certainly. And you know respiratory system and "respirer," words of the same route, just mean that they need to take a breath now and then as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My apologies to the booths and to the court reporter and to the Chamber. There is no evidence in the record that General Gotovina had any knowledge of crimes that was not known to the civilian and military authorities. In fact, the evidence has been the opposite, that General Gotovina would have been relying on the civilian and military authorities for his information and not the other way around. And with respect to imposing immediate disciplinary measures, we have already discussed the fact of the increase of 151 per cent in the third quarter. We are thus left to speculate as to what the necessary and reasonable measure is that the Prosecution believes General Gotovina failed to take. Having failed to put that specific issue to Mr. Theunens or Mr. Lausic or any other relevant witness, having decided to abandon the testimony of General Pringle, we are now going to be left with speculation argued by Prosecution counsel as to what a reasonable and necessary measure would have been. We note the potential that the Prosecution is going to rely on a hypothetical answer given by General Forand at 4535 of the transcript about removing a commander in the event that orders were not being implemented. However, we note that there is no evidence in the record of any question having been put to General Forand or any other witness about General Gotovina's specific circumstances and whether in the specific circumstances of this case, that would have been an appropriate measure. Furthermore, we note that in the one instances of a commander being unable to implement the orders, that would be the 134th Home Guard brigade which I have mentioned already, the Split Military District demobilized virtually the entire 134th Home Guard Brigade. And it can be hardly said that the Prosecution has proven that that was not a necessary and reasonable measure with respect to that unit. The Prosecution, given the fact that there is no evidence that after the 18th August General Gotovina would have this any information that the measures he had taken were not effective, the Prosecution is left to show that there were other necessary and reasonable measures which could have been taken and which would have stopped criminal activity before the 18th of August. We submit to you, Your Honours, that there is no evidence in the record to support such speculation by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I will actually try to wrap up before then, so I thank the interpreters for sacrificing some time. With respect to the issue of the military police command and control, that has been a topic which has been debated at length and which the -- the Trial Chamber does not need us to go over again. Suffice it to say, that is it clear on the evidence, and there is no evidence capable of prove beyond a reasonable doubt that General Gotovina was in command of the military police in its crime prevention, crime investigation, and crime prosecution functions. You had the opportunity to see Mr. Lausic. You have seen the documents. And it has not been challenged by the Prosecution that in fact Mr. Lausic, through Major Juric, was exercising command and control over the military police in those functions, and more importantly, or just as importantly, that is entirely consistent with the system that had been set up on the 2nd of August, the plans that had been detailed on the 3rd of August, and the orders that were issued by General Lausic regarding reporting from the field and the fact that the military police in its reporting would be reporting directly to him through Major Juric and not reporting to General Gotovina. Therefore, the evidence in the record thus far is that orders were issued by General Lausic through Major Juric, and reports were sent back up that same chain with relation to crime prevention, crime investigation, and crime prosecution. The evidence also is -- I should say, there is no evidence that any orders were issued by General Gotovina to the military police regarding crime prevention, crime investigation, and crime prosecution, nor were reports sent to him on those counts. The Prosecution is left with arguing that General Gotovina received daily reports, the regular daily reports of the 72nd MP Battalion, but we note that the Chamber should pay particular attention to whom those reports were sent. They were sent to a wide distribution list, including military prosecutors, garrison commanders, political affairs officers, et cetera, yet the Prosecution wouldn't allege that the military prosecutor's office had military police under its command and control. We submit that the issue is clear and that there has been no evidence to support a theory. In fact, I should point out that it would actually contradict the Prosecution's own in-house expert should the Prosecution now argue that there was a dual command over the military police. Mr. Theunens was quite clear in his expert report and in his oral testimony that in the HV, including in the military police, the principle of unity of command ruled, which meant there is one commander, or not two commanders issuing orders on the same subjects. Given Mr. Theunens' position, we submit that if there is one commander in fact for military -- for crime prevention, crime investigation, and crime prosecution, that the only conclusion that can be drawn is that that commander was Mate Lausic. With respect to the murder counts, the Defence requests that these Counts which are Counts 6 and 7 be dismissed and it is the Defence's working understanding that such a dismissal would encompass the ten specific killing incidents identified in the joinder indictment along with the entire 337 alleged victims now listed in Appendix C to the Prosecution's further clarification of identity of victims. The first reason the counts fail is because there has been no evidence that General Gotovina knew or had reason to know that his subordinates committed murder and that is the mens rea standard established by the Appeals Chamber in the Oric appeals decision of December 2007. It is not sufficient under that Appeals Chamber judgment that General Gotovina may have been aware of the disposal of dead bodies by sanitation crews, since this does not establish either, A, that the deaths were unlawful killings constituting murder as distinct from combat-related deaths or lawful killings, or, B, that General Gotovina's subordinates were responsible. Now the Defence has been left throughout the pre-trial and trial ... now the Defence has been left throughout the pre-trial and trial phase, and so has the Trial Chamber for that matter, to speculate as to what the Prosecution's theory is of General Gotovina's mens rea with respect to killings. Based on a review of the Prosecutor's opening statement, it is our belief that the Prosecution intends to rely on sanitation reports issued to the Split Military District or from the Split Military District, and these would be Prosecution Exhibits P507, and D1057. However, on this score, it is important to note the cross-examination of Mr. Theunens on this point. Mr. Theunens had a specific section in his report entitled "Notice to General Gotovina of crimes." And based on that, he was cross-examined about the fact that nothing in his report indicated that General Gotovina had any notice of crimes -- I should say of murder having been committed. The Chamber will recall that Mr. Theunens was given the third session of one day and was given the opportunity overnight to review his report and to review the Prosecution's database to see if he could find any document which would indicate that General Gotovina had notice of murder. And Mr. Theunens, when he came back to court the next morning - this is at transcript page 12570, lines 6 to 16, 12609, lines 1 to 6, and lines 13 to 25 - Mr. Theunens acknowledged that he had found no written evidence or other evidence of any notice of murder to General Gotovina. That is independent in addition to its importance because it comes from the OTP's in-house expert. It is also important to note that Mr. Theunens cited the sanitation reports in his report, and this would be at pages 167 of the Theunens' report, which is 427 of the PDF, page 241 which is page 501 in the PDF, pages 245 to 246 which is pages 505 to 506 of the PDF, and page 262 which is page 522 of the PDF, and specifically Exhibits P507 and D1057, upon which we expect the Prosecution to rely for mens rea for murder are in Theunens' report. So we are left with the situation apparently, unless this is an new theory that comes up in response, that the Prosecution's in-house expert himself had the sanitation documents not only at his disposal but cited them in his report, had two days, or I should say an afternoon and an evening to consider whether he could find any notice of murder. And he, himself, didn't think that sanitation reports amount to mens rea notice of murder. We submit to you, Your Honours, that if the OTP's own in-house expert did not believe that the sanitation documents cited in his own report constitute notice of murder, it is unclear how the Office of the Prosecutor expects the Trial Chamber to rely on these same sanitation documents as capable of proving beyond a reasonable doubt General Gotovina's knowledge of murder. There is no -- moving forward, there is no JCE catchall here. There is no basis to hold General Gotovina liable for murders as a foreseeable consequence of a JCE for the reasons previously argued; namely, that there is insufficient proof of the JCE. We also wish to rely on the Strugar Rule 98 bis decision which permits partial dismissal of Counts. And as Mr. Akhavan indicated in that decision, the Trial Chamber permitted the dismissal of certain structures at that point in the case because damage to those structures had not been proven. We submit that in respect to the murders, the Trial Chamber should take the same approach that the Strugar Trial Chamber did in the Rule 98 bis decision and dismiss the following -- first of all, all of the murder allegations as it relates to General Gotovina do to the mens rea failure. But then specifically -- and we can provide a written submission on this if the Chamber desires. But with respect to the following cases, there has been no evidence presented at all by the Prosecution relating to some alleged murder victims identified in its further clarification schedule, no witnesses testified about the alleged circumstances, no witness statements were admitted discussing the alleged circumstances, no autopsy or other report was admitted concerning 87 specific instances. And I can read out the numbers in the further clarification, which is 9 to 11, 21, 23, 24, 29, 31 through 34, 36, 38, 39, 41, 77, 79, 80, 82, 83, 85, 108, 109, 115, 116, 118, 131, 132, 135, 140, 141, numbers 164 through 179, number 192, 194, 210, 223, 225, 262, 276, 283 through 285, 300, 301, 303, 304, 308 through 315, 318 through 320, 322, and 324 through 337. There's also undisputed evidence tendered through Dr. Clark of hospital patients that it was apparent that several of the alleged murder victims identified in the Prosecution's further clarification schedule who were in fact patients from the Knin hospital who had no apparent indication of having been murdered, these five instances are in the clarification schedule and are numbered 12, 234, 239, 243, and 270. With respect to cases where the cause of death was unascertained or undetermined, those are 37 specific incidents. They are 15, 16, 51, 55, 58, 59 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 65, 104, 113, 191, 193, 197, 200, 202, 205 through 207, 213 through 220, 224, 226, 228 through to 230, 238, 240, 241, 264, 268, 288, 297, and 302. In addition, there are some incidents -- we note again that the Chamber has now given us five weeks to investigate the rest of these alleged killings, so this is a tentative review. But the Prosecution in the following instances has not established any evidence of a superior/subordinate relationship to scheduled killing incident 4, scheduled killing incident 5, scheduled killing 7, scheduled killing 9. Scheduled killing 10 was an incident that did not take place in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. Scheduled killing 1, 6, and scheduled killing 8.1, we state should be dismissed because the evidence contradicted a finding of murder, for example 8.1 was an indication -- or the evidence was that the person committed suicide. And finally the evidence in the record with respect to the following incidents indicates that an investigation and Prosecution was done with respect to scheduled killing 8.2 which is Uros Saric and 8.3 Uros Ognjenovic, the Varivode incident which is further clarification 95 through 103, and Sava Babic which is further clarification incident 7. In summation, and as our prayer for relief, Your Honours, we ask, that the following be dismissed: All Article 5 crime against humanity charges fail because there was no widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population. This would result in a dismissal of persecutions under 5(h), deportation under Article 5(d), inhumane act, forcible transfer under Article 5(i), murder under Article 5(a), and more generally, inhumane acts under Article 5(i). Count 1 fails because Operation Storm was lawful under the laws of war, so it does not constitute a crime against humanity. There was no discriminatory intent with regard to the purpose of Operation Storm. There was no discriminatory intent with regards to the burnings and lootings. Counts 2 and 3 also fail because civilians did not flee and there's been no evidence that they fled due to unlawful shelling. Notwithstanding lawful shelling, civilians did not flee because of panic arising from combat operations. Collection centres did not constitute forcible transfer. Counts 4 through 9 fail because there's been no evidence that General Gotovina had the intent to commit crimes against humanity or war crimes through destruction or pillage of property or that he made a significant contribution to the commission of such crimes. In fact the undisputed evidence has been that General Gotovina issued orders and took measures to stop such criminal activity. There is thus no policy of acquiescence. Even if the Trial Chamber were to find that they're generally was, there is no evidence that General Gotovina was part of such an acquiescence. Therefore, there is no JCE after Operation Storm. This is a case of command responsibility, and the evidence has been that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures against his subordinates. The Prosecution contends apparently that he did not take enough necessary and reasonable measures, but the Prosecution has failed to adduce evidence of what that necessary and reasonable measure or measures with have been. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecutor has failed it present evidence of General Gotovina's criminal liability on all counts of the joinder indictment. Accordingly, we respectfully request that this Trial Chamber enter a judgement of acquittal on all counts. On behalf of Mr. Akhavan and Mr. Kehoe, I thank you for your attention. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Before we take a break, I with like it put a few short questions, not to enter a debate, but just to seek a clarification. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite the Cermak Defence to make submissions under Rule 98 bis. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is the application on behalf of Ivan Cermak to dismiss the charges at the close of the Prosecution case against him. All the evidence has been heard at this stage relevant to this application. The evidence won't get any better. But does it leave the Court with a case that has been proved against the accused Mr. Cermak? That is the issue here. Rule 98 bis is a power granted to the Court to be exercised in an appropriate case. We submit this is just such a case. An indicator as to the kind of test to be applied has been given on behalf of my previous co-defendant's counsel. An indicator can also be how accurate have the assertions been by the Prosecutor in relation to the allegations in the indictment, how well-founded have they been upon the evidence that the Court has received. The crucial thing is for the court to assess what exactly is the evidence in relation to the indictment at this stage, not assertions or allegations, but the evidence in the case. I'm going to turn to the paragraphs of the indictment that are -- call for a submission such as this. The first is paragraph 7, which deals with the Article 7(3), command responsibility notion of the case. And there are some universal truths that are well known concerning command responsibility, as well as some specific matters that also need to be considered, in relation to a particular defendant. I'll deal with the universal truths, first of all. There is an need for effective control of subordinates. Without effective control, there is no duty on behalf of a person to act. The superior and subordinate relationship between the accused and the perpetrator of crimes, did the superior know or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit or had committed underlying crime? Did the superior fail to prevent or punish? The key to those universal truths are the superior/subordinate relationship. There are further aspects to this that need to be considered in the kind of case that the Court has been it, concerning Ivan Cermak. And I will run through those briefly. Did the superior have material abilities to prevent subordinate offences or punish subordinate offenders? The Delic and Limaj case express that. Mere influence over people is not enough or even great influence, or other expressions of influence turning to the Kordic, Celebici, and Limaj cases. The superior must have capacity to issue binding instruction and enforce compliance with orders. Coordination obviously is not of that kind of authority. We turn to the Celebici case for that proposition. An accused if perceived or thought to have command authority, doesn't lead to the conclusion of fact that he had in fact effective control; Celebici Halilovic cases. The ability of a superior to maintain and enforce compliance, not just convince or sway decisions; the Oric case. De jure status does not of itself create a strict liability. We return to the Oric and Halilovic cases again. All of the cases state cite there is a need for de facto effective control. And looking at someone who is a civilian, he is required to a degree of control over subordinates similar to that of a military commander in an analogous position. We see that in Aleksovski and the Kajelijeli case. Issuing orders may not indicate actual authority. That is a very important matter to bear in mind in this case, see the Kordic, Halilovic, and Oric case. Lack of compliance of orders by others may indicate a lack of authority with the accused. Look at the Strugar case. And the types of orders issued by an accused may be important. What is their purpose rather than the mere fact of issuing an order. Binding combat orders are different from humanitarian-type orders. See the Halilovic case, Kordic, Blaskic cases. In our submission, those additional factors to the universal truths make common sense to be applied in a case where you considering effective control, and we ask the Court to bear that into in mind when considering the evidence at this stage, in relation to Mr. Cermak. Let me just cite a few passages from a couple of cases here, which drive this home. In the Celebici case it was stated: "Great care must be taken lest an injustice be committed in holding individuals responsible for the acts of others in situations where the link of control is absent or too remote." In the Blaskic appeals decision it was stated: "The appellant did not enjoy or exercise effective command and control over all units nominally subordinated to him." And turning finally on this section of my submissions to the Kovacka appeals: "Not every position of authority and influence necessarily leads to superior responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute." So let us turn now to paragraph 7 specifically and consider a number of matters that arise from the language of the paragraph. In it is cited the need for effective control over members of the HV units or elements attached to the Knin garrison. I'm not going to read all the language out in full, as it would take too much time. But let us consider, first of all, in that aspect of the paragraph the Croatian army units and the allegation that Ivan Cermak had effective control over all those units specified. I will remind the Court of the evidence of the Prosecution expert who is an employee of the Prosecutor and was questioned about this paragraph in cross-examination by me. I put to him at transcript page 12990: "You have read the indictment. I will then paraphrase. Paragraph 7 describes Ivan Cermak as possessing effective control over members of the Croatian army units or elements who comprised or were attached to or operated in the Knin garrison." I read out those units within paragraph 7 of the indictment, and I put to him: "But looking at all these Military District documents, we've looked at a few here which go to a particular issue. But there are, as you know, thousands, in relation to all those units. General Cermak is copied in on a handful of matters, isn't he?" The expert answered: "It is correct. And I think it is visible through my report that there are very few orders by General Gotovina to the Knin garrison command or the Knin garrison commander during the time-period General Cermak is the commander of the Knin garrison." I put to him: "My question is about General Cermak having effective control over all those units. They're all operating every day in relation to their activities, where they go, what they do, completely independently and without General Cermak. That's right, isn't it? What I'm putting to is that paragraph 7 of this indictment doesn't fit with your expert's report." "That may well be possible," was the answer. On that passage of the indictment that I read, I then put: "In relation to paragraph 7, which asserts that Ivan Cermak possessed in various structures of power," and I cited the matter from paragraph 7 and when went on to say, " ... in fact, not borne out by your expert's report and indeed all the documents that you have seen, it's right, isn't it? I'm right." And the answer was: "I mean, I haven't addressed effective control. In fact, yeah, I mean I haven't addressed effective control, and I haven't seen any material or, I mean, documents on that aspect concerning the role of General Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison." This was the expert who described himself as an expert on command and control in one of the very first questions that I asked of him in cross-examination. Your Honour, in our submission, the truth was clear in this expert's mind, as to what he had looked at, as to what he seen, that he could in no way positively express a support for paragraph 7 of this indictment. It was not founded upon the substance of reality, of the documents of the case, nor the military function of the Split Military District. It was a paragraph inserted into the indictment at an alarmingly high and overstated way, that, in our submission, underlines the need for Rule 98 bis to be applied in the Defence of Ivan Cermak. Let us look, then, aside from what Mr. Theunens admitted, to what we have seen in the evidence concerning the Croatian military concerned. In three hours, I do not know whether I have the time to express all the matters that could be raised. I will attempt to do so. However, I ask the Court to bear in mind the very clear cross-examinations that we submit have taken place here, where we have put our case fairly and squarely, and we have produced and analysed the documents in the trial to a level where the Court has a very clear understanding, we submit, of the Defence issues concerning these matters in the trial. First of all, the function in which Mr. Cermak was placed, that of the garrison commander, it is very important for the Court to note that that had no operational function as a part of the military structure. The role of the garrison commander, in D34, Exhibit D34, is stated: "The garrison HQ commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian military units except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order, and discipline at the garrison headquarters, et cetera." Mr. Theunens was cross-examined by me at length concerning those issues, and I refer the Court to the fact of his agreement with me as to the nature of the role of the garrison commander. In relation to the authority within the military of General Cermak, the Court is alerted to the fact that the Prosecution have relied on a few orders ostensibly showing authority or command without putting before the Court the full story of those orders, and we stress that, because orders seeking supplemental troops to the garrison issued by General Cermak were actually shown upon more detailed research of documents within the Prosecution Rule 65 ter collection and exhibited by us to have been failures of the exercise of his authority and command. And I refer the Court to the issue concerning Captain Jonjic of the logistics brigade, who was ordered by General Cermak to work for him. His commander complained, and eventually General Cermak had to seek the intervention of General Gotovina on that matter. Your Honours, a case built upon scraps of orders that have no context of themselves beyond what they say, in our submission, is a very dangerous way to approach a criminal trial. This Court, if handled appropriately and correctly by the Prosecution, should have been given the full story in relation to the limitations of the command and authority and control that General Cermak had. We move from there, the Jonjic orders, to the request for the garrison to receive further troops to help in the clearing up of the town. Again, one knows from the evidence that was introduced by the Defence that this was something that required a further subordination of those troops to General Cermak. He was unable to do it. And I remind the Court of my cross-examination of the witness Liborius where the full story on this matter was put before the Court to show the limitations of Mr. Cermak's authority. And what are these orders? I have described them as scraps of paper. And I do that with a sense of justice about it, because we are dealing here with the command and control of military units alleged to have committed crimes, and what is being put before the Court are non-operational orders, as a symbol to support the argument of the Prosecutor that General Cermak had effective control. In our submission, they show nothing of the sort, and that is why at the start of my opening I referred the court to the passages from decisions whereby the quality and nature of orders issued has been considered by the courts to be an important feature to demonstrate whether an accused had effective control or not. The difference between combat operation orders and the difference between orders concerning fish farms, orders concerning men to clear the streets, and the order to receive the assistance of a logistics captain are of a very different nature to the kind of orders that are required to found the foundation in relation to the allegations of serious crimes in this indictment. The other matters, and again I refer the Court to them, is the UNCRO orders. These have been cited many times by the Prosecutor as being relied upon to demonstrate effective control - and at this stage I'm just dealing with the Croatian military units, but within that organisation one could consider the military police - and it is quite clear that those are the kind of order that is not arising out of the issues necessary to show effective command responsibility of all those units within paragraph 7, but they fit into that category of order issued to assist the international community and are of not the same type or nature to illustrate the power over the subordinates within Croatian military units that needs to be proven by the Prosecutor to establish effective control. Not only that, one can see from the history of those documents, again, not put into full context by the Prosecutor, but put into full context by the Defence, how General Cermak was unable to fulfil his obligation to help the UN recover those vehicles and required intervention so that his order that he had drafted was reproduced and disseminated to other units within the Split Military District. In summary, if one looks at the documents relied upon by the Prosecutor to establish effective control and command of units, they show that those documents issued by General Cermak were non-operational, logistical documents, and indicative of a non-operational role. Let us consider now the duty to discipline within the Croatian military. Reliance was put upon a document by Mr. Theunens as an example of a garrison commander disciplining a member of the Croatian military, D1001, exhibit, to demonstrate this kind of authority would have been available to General Cermak. What was missing crucially from the information before the Court and which I cross-examined him upon was the fact that that was an example of the garrison commander in Split disciplining his own subordinate. Transcript pages 12955 to 7. Your Honours, in our submission, the Court has to be concerned about a case structured and put before it where such glaring inaccuracies have been used to support the allegations. In our submission, that should -- could cause the Court at this stage to have serious alarm bells ringing, concerning the nature of this Prosecution against Mr. Cermak. Let us turn now to the Code of Military Discipline. That, at Articles 19 and 27, gives the responsibility of General Cermak as with any other commander within the Croatian army to discipline a subordinate. Under Article 26 there is the power to discipline an individual brought before him not of his organic unit, in which required and necessary measures are desirable or needed to maintain order and discipline. But as far as the matter goes, that is it. He can discipline his subordinates. There is no evidence in this case that his subordinates have committed any of the crimes on the indictment, and the Court is reminded of the evidence in support of his subordinates, which are the manning documents, issued periodically to demonstrate the number of soldiers within each unit of the Split Military District. The document filed for June the 28th, 2005 [sic], before Operation Storm demonstrated there were three people. The document filed at the end of August 30th of 1995, after Operation Storm, showed the garrison had nine soldiers within it, and the same number at the end of September 1995. So that is it, on the level, to show the extent of the authority within the garrison of General Cermak. Those nine subordinates, none of whom have been proved to have committed any of the crimes alleged. Court will be reminded of the many documents within the Military District concerning operations, communications, steps to be taken by units, et cetera, none of which were copied in to General Cermak and demonstrate that he was part of the overall structure with the necessary position to have effective control over those units. It was conceded by Mr. Theunens that for any military entity to function, there was the need for reports, there was the need for lines of reporting, there would be orders issued, there would be the means of communication. It was quite clear that within the documents that we have seen that General Cermak was only ever an occasional receiver of such information. Well, how, we ask the question, can any effective control be exerted over those units in paragraph 7 with that kind of structure and establishment? We were looking forward to hearing from General Pringle, and we were prepared to cross-examine him on the materials at our disposal that had been put before Mr. Theunens. That opportunity having been denied, the Court is left with Mr. Theunens' evidence on the matter, and, in our submission, it clearly underlined the accuracy of our submission. All those orders that the Court will have had referred to or seen, referred to in Mr. Theunens' report or seen during the evidence itself, none of the operational orders can be said to have been forwarded or included as information to General Cermak. One just has to look at the weekly and other reports that were submitted. What the Court does know, however, from evidence in this case, and that is an indicator as much as anything else of the nature and role that he had within the events outlined in this indictment was that he was undertaking matters which were more closely related to the civilian dimension of life in Knin than the military life in Knin. And that is a very important distinction, which the authorities of the Tribunal have pointed out, and at this stage, this Court is quite clearly in possession of a sufficient amount of information to determine that they are able to make a finding that his role was entirely, as described by him in his interviews, as described by countless witnesses, his role was the normalisation of live in Knin, coordinating civilian authorities which is one of the doubts of a garrison commander within its regulations, with the role of helping establish civilian life, and the plethora of orders and letters that indicate that that was how he spent his time, in our submission, clearly demonstrate his role and the extent of his authority. The fact that members of the international community wrongly perceived him to be a military governor or in charge of the whole area, and in charge of units does not prove the case against him. This Court has been able to look behind the extent of the knowledge that General Forand, others had at the time, and seen the inner workings of Knin, Knin civil life, as well as the Knin military structure through the Split Military District, as well as the Croatian military structure, so that this Court is not bound by the impressions held at the time, and I don't say that they weren't genuine impressions. I accept them entirely as being sincerely held impressions of those witnesses called by the international community. But those witnesses, virtually to a man, accepted that they did not know enough or sufficiently about the workings of either the Croatian government, the Croatian military, or Croatian civil life to actually be in possession of knowledge that would be safe for this Court to determine the matter upon. Even the fact that they may have been believed that Mr. Cermak held himself out in such a position is not determinative of the matter. This Court has seen the evidence that was in operation at that time that clearly defined what he was doing, what he could do, and what he couldn't do, so when he said to General Forand, We will issue an order to return your vehicles and have this matter investigated, the fact that that was said by him is not necessarily determinative of the issue of actual authority and control. Because Your Honours know that behind that statement lay a different picture. It actually concealed a picture of a man issuing orders for banks, bakeries, trout farms, accommodation, logistical orders, and his very limited orders that he did issue in relation to the matter of the theft of UN vehicles were the only extent of those orders of a similar nature. And that's very, very important, Your Honours, because even though he may have held himself out or people had expectations of him, the fact of the matter is that that does not determine the matter. And if Your Honours were not in possession of other information, other evidence in this case that threw a light upon the, truth you would be able to disregard my submissions. But, clearly, in the evidence in this case, we have been able to present to you documents and evidence that showed the true extent of that authority.

utterances.text: And I remind the Court that several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. That several international witnesses all expressed, and can you see in those reports that they were writing at that time, doubts about whether he could deliver what he said he could deliver. In our submission, this impression evidence, for that is what it is, has been countered by the truth and the facts of the evidence that shows otherwise. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I have reached a natural break, and it's quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Before we adjourn, just two brief matters. The first is that I inform the parties that the request for certification for an appeal to the clarification issue has been signed this morning and has been filed this morning, granting a certificate. That's one. Second, without, at this moment expressing any opinion about whether Rule 98 bis allows for a partial acquittal within a Count, even if that would not be possible, that, of course, does not prevent the Prosecution from considering whether all elements in a Count or all offences charged within a Count could stand. Mr. Misetic has given you a long list of persons who -- for whom there is evidence, for example, that they died, but that other evidence would suggest that it may have been suicide rather than murder. We have heard of hospital patients, we have heard -- at least evidence has been presented on persons that, as the Defence evidence suggests, may have died outside the territorial scope of the indictment. The Chamber would very much appreciate if the Prosecution would pay serious attention to specifically those cases mentioned and to see to what extent it still has a firm -- I'm not talking about the Counts as a whole, but in these specific cases, whether the Prosecution takes the view that it is very likely that the Chamber would be convinced that, for example, this person did not commit suicide but was murdered, to seriously think about these matters so as to be able to focus, if there will be any Defence case, to focus on those cases where not any strong suggestive Defence evidence exists.
